chunks.title: What glaucoma is & aqueous dynamics
chunks.tldr: Chronic optic neuropathy: disc cupping + field loss, usually with raised IOP. ~60 million worldwide; half undiagnosed; leading cause of preventable blindness in the US. POAG commonest in blacks and whites; angle closure dominates in East Asia/Inuit; NTG commonest in Japan. Aqueous: ~250 µL, made at ~2.5 µL/min by ciliary epithelium; high ascorbate/lactate, low protein. Exit: trabecular → Schlemm → collectors → episcleral veins (main resistance = juxtacanalicular tissue), plus uveoscleral. Episcleral venous pressure sets the IOP floor.
points: Mechanism of vision loss = retinal ganglion cell apoptosis.
Screen everyone >35 with disc check + tonometry; blacks 2-yearly from 35, yearly from 50; first-degree relatives.
chunks.hook: In through the ciliary body, out through the meshwork.

cards.q: Site of greatest resistance to conventional aqueous outflow?
cards.a: Juxtacanalicular trabecular tissue next to the inner wall of Schlemm's canal.

chunks.title: Tonometry, gonioscopy, disc & fields
chunks.tldr: Goldmann applanation: normal 11–21 mmHg (elderly up to 24); thick cornea overestimates, thin cornea underestimates (Pascal DCT avoids this). Diurnal swings; 1/3–1/2 of POAG have normal IOP at first check. Gonioscopy: see scleral spur/TM = open; only Schwalbe's line = narrow; nothing = closed. Hyperopes narrow, myopes wide. Disc: RNFL thinning first, then enlarged vertical cup, notching (inferior > superior), disc haemorrhage, nasal vessel shift, bean-pot cup, asymmetry. Fields: central 30°, Bjerrum/arcuate, Seidel, nasal step, temporal and central islands last; white-on-white SAP misses until ~40% ganglion loss (SWAP, FDT earlier).
points: Acuity is a poor guide — a patient can be 6/6 with a 5° field (legally blind).

cards.q: Effect of a thin central cornea on Goldmann IOP?

cards.a: Thinning of the peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer.

chunks.title: Glaucoma drops
chunks.tldr: Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluproost) nightly — ↑uveoscleral outflow; 1st line. SE: red eye, iris darkening, lash growth, periorbital fat loss/pigment, CME/uveitis/HSV reactivation. β-blockers (timolol) ↓production; avoid in asthma/COPD, heart block; betaxolol β1-selective, weaker. α2-agonists: brimonidine (↓production + ↑uveoscleral; allergy; apnoea in infants), apraclonidine (post-laser spikes; tachyphylaxis). Topical CAIs dorzolamide/brinzolamide (bitter taste). Miotics pilocarpine (↑trabecular; brow ache, myopia, RD). Oral acetazolamide 250 mg qds/500 mg IV: paraesthesia, kidney stones, hypokalaemia, sulfa allergy. Hyperosmotics: glycerol 1 mL/kg oral (care in diabetics), IV mannitol.
points: Fixed combos with timolol reduce drop burden.
chunks.hook: PGA opens the back door (uveoscleral); pilocarpine opens the front door (trabecular).

chunks.title: Laser & surgery
chunks.tldr: YAG peripheral iridotomy: fixes pupil block (argon in dark irides); prophylaxis in narrow angles; argon iridoplasty if PI fails/can't be done. Laser trabeculoplasty (ALT/SLT) → can be first-line in POAG; effect fades over 2–5 y. Trabeculectomy ± MMC/5-FU (scarring risk: young, black, secondary, previous surgery) — best IOP drop; risks bleb leak, blebitis/endophthalmitis, hypotony maculopathy, cataract. Tubes (Baerveldt/Molteno non-valved, Ahmed valved) for high-risk eyes. Non-penetrating (deep sclerectomy, viscocanalostomy) safer, less effect; MIGS. Goniotomy/trabeculotomy for congenital. Cyclodestruction (diode/cryo) for refractory/blind painful eyes.
chunks.hook: Pupil block → hole in the iris; open angle → laser the meshwork or build a new drain.

chunks.title: POAG, NTG & ocular hypertension
chunks.tldr: POAG: 1.3–2% >40 y, 4.7% >75; 4× more common and 6× more blinding in blacks; family history; myocilin (chr 1) in juvenile OAG. Asymptomatic, bilateral. Each 1 mmHg ↓ ≈ 10% ↓ progression risk (EMGT); advanced → target <15. NTG: IOP ≤21 but damage; vascular (vasospasm, low CSF pressure), optineurin (chr 10); disc haemorrhages common; exclude diurnal spikes, thin cornea, previous steroids/uveitis, intermittent closure, compressive lesions; 30% IOP ↓ helps (CNTGS). OHT: raised IOP, normal disc/field → 1–2%/yr convert (higher if high IOP, thin CCT, big cup, haemorrhage); OHTS: treatment halves conversion.
chunks.hook: Normal pressure doesn't rule out glaucoma — look at the disc.

cards.a: Treating ocular hypertension reduced conversion to POAG (~9.5% → 4.4% at 5 y); thin CCT is a strong risk factor.

cards.q: Gene linked to some familial normal-tension glaucoma?

chunks.title: Acute angle closure
chunks.tldr: Small hyperopic eye, big old lens, women, East Asian/Inuit. Trigger: dim light, mydriatics, anticholinergics (antidepressants, nebulisers, decongestants), topiramate (secondary). Pupil block → iris bombé → IOP 60–80. Painful red eye, halos, nausea/vomiting (mimics abdomen), steamy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, shallow AC; gonioscope the fellow eye. Rx: IV/oral acetazolamide + topical β-blocker, apraclonidine/brimonidine, steroid, ± hyperosmotic; pilocarpine 2% after ~30 min (ischaemic sphincter won't respond earlier); then YAG PI both eyes; surgical iridectomy if PI fails; lens extraction increasingly used.
points: Iritis: small pupil, normal/low IOP, more photophobia. Conjunctivitis: discharge, no pain or vision loss.
chunks.hook: Vomiting old lady with a red eye and mid-dilated pupil — check the pressure, not the abdomen.

cards.q: Why delay pilocarpine in acute angle closure?
cards.a: The ischaemic iris sphincter won't respond until IOP has been lowered.

cards.q: Definitive treatment after breaking an acute attack?
cards.a: Laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes.

chunks.title: Subacute & chronic angle closure, plateau iris
chunks.tldr: Subacute (intermittent): evening episodes of ache, blur, halos that resolve overnight; PAS accumulate → PI. Chronic angle closure: creeping PAS, gradual IOP rise, looks like POAG; gonioscopy is the key → PI first, then drops; surgery often needed; phaco + IOL helps if ≤2 quadrants PAS; no strong miotics before PI. Plateau iris: anteriorly placed ciliary processes; normal central AC depth but angle crowds on dilation despite a patent PI → iridoplasty or long-term miotics; younger patients. Nomenclature: 'angle-closure glaucoma' only once disc/field damage exists.
chunks.hook: Angle still closes after a good PI? Think plateau iris.

cards.a: Anteriorly positioned ciliary processes push the peripheral iris forward, causing angle crowding on dilation without significant pupil block.

chunks.title: Congenital glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Primary congenital (angle dysgenesis) or with anomalies: Axenfeld-Rieger, Peters, aniridia; syndromes: Sturge-Weber, NF1, Lowe, rubella, Marfan. 50% at birth, 80% by 1 y. Triad: epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm; then cloudy cornea, Haab striae (Descemet breaks), buphthalmos (corneal diameter >11.5 mm in newborn = significant), deep AC, early cupping (reversible). Treatment is surgical: goniotomy (clear cornea) or trabeculotomy.
chunks.hook: Watery, light-shy baby with big cloudy corneas = congenital glaucoma, not blocked duct.

cards.a: Horizontal/curvilinear breaks in Descemet's membrane from corneal stretching in infantile glaucoma.

chunks.title: Pigmentary & pseudoexfoliation glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Pigment dispersion: young myopic men 25–40, deep AC, concave (posterior bowing) iris rubs zonules → Krukenberg spindle, mid-peripheral radial transillumination defects, heavily pigmented TM (Sampaolesi line); IOP spikes after exercise or dilation; 10% glaucoma by 5 y. PI flattens iris; SLT; often surgery. PXF: elderly, Scandinavia, LOXL1; white fibrillar flakes on anterior lens ('target'), pupil margin; also systemic. 5% glaucoma at 5 y, 15% at 10 y; higher IOP, worse course; weak zonules → cataract surgery complications.
points: True exfoliation (glassblower's cataract) = infrared-induced capsular delamination — different.
chunks.hook: Young myope, IOP up after jogging = pigment dispersion.

cards.q: Three signs of pigment dispersion syndrome?
cards.a: Krukenberg spindle, mid-peripheral radial iris transillumination defects, dense trabecular pigmentation.

chunks.title: Lens, uveitic, ICE & traumatic glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Lens: anterior dislocation/intumescent lens → pupil block (remove lens); phacolytic — leaky hypermature lens protein clogs TM (no keratic precipitates, white flecks) → lower IOP, steroid, remove lens. Uveitic: TM blockage, trabeculitis, steroid response, PAS, seclusio pupillae → iris bombé; worst offenders Fuchs, HLA-B27, herpes; avoid miotics, use mydriatics. Tumour (melanoma), ciliary body swelling (topiramate, after VR surgery) → secondary closure. ICE: young women, unilateral, beaten-metal endothelium, corectopia/polycoria, PAS. Trauma: hyphaema (worse with rebleed; sickle!), angle recession (late, deeper AC), PAS from flat AC.
chunks.hook: Old eye on a 'dead' cataract becomes red and hard = phacolytic.

cards.q: Clinical clue to angle recession glaucoma?
cards.a: History of blunt trauma, deeper AC than fellow eye, wide ciliary body band on gonioscopy — glaucoma may appear years later.
Young adult women, unilateral; corneal endothelial abnormality ('hammered silver'), iris atrophy/corectopia/polycoria, PAS and glaucoma.

chunks.title: Malignant, neovascular, episcleral & steroid glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Ciliary block (malignant) glaucoma: after surgery in eyes with closed/narrow angles — aqueous misdirected into vitreous, shallow central AND peripheral AC with high IOP despite patent PI, myopic shift. Rx: cycloplegics/mydriatics (atropine), aqueous suppressants, hyperosmotics; YAG hyaloidotomy, vitrectomy. NVG: ischaemic DR, CRVO, carotid disease → fibrovascular membrane → zipped-shut angle; anti-VEGF + PRP, atropine + steroid, tube or cyclodestruction. Raised episcleral venous pressure: Sturge-Weber, carotid-cavernous fistula — meds can't go below EVP. Steroid-induced: topical > periocular/intraocular > systemic; ~weeks; worse with family history of POAG.
chunks.hook: Flat AC + high IOP after trab + patent PI = aqueous misdirection → atropine.

cards.q: Medical treatment of malignant (ciliary block) glaucoma?
cards.a: Cycloplegic-mydriatics (atropine), aqueous suppressants and hyperosmotic agents.
